fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Blocking ciliary motion with ciliobrevin sharply decreases Anthrobot motility, showing that their locomotion is driven by surface cilia.

fields.value: We administered the efficient blocker of cilia motion, ciliobrevin,[ 20 ] and observed the expected drastic decrease in motility (See Figure S6, Supporting Information), confirming that the motility of Anthrobots is cilia‐driven.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The perturbation and motility readout are highly direct. Existing measurements support ciliary dependence, but limited controls prevent a fully clean causal attribution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate within-condition changes in ciliary beat and bot displacement after ciliobrevin, with vehicle controls and viability measurements.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ciliobrevin may have off-target or toxicity effects.

Dose-response and washout evidence may not be public.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A paired speed change under a cilia-motion blocker is a direct test of how these bots move. The paper reports a drastic decrease and does not release the tracks. The pharmacological contrast is clean enough to be decisive once the numbers exist in public form; they do not yet.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure speed before and after ciliobrevin, with a vehicle control, on the same bots. A sharp drop that reverses the way ciliary beat stops, and that spares non-ciliary readouts, would support cilia-driven locomotion; unchanged speed would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Dose, sample size and the pre-drug baseline are not in an open table.

Ciliobrevin inhibits cytoplasmic dynein, so a motility drop is not cilia-exclusive without a beat assay on the same bots.

The ciliobrevin speeds are in a supporting figure and are not deposited.
